title: SDK Governance Rubric and Intake Playbook for Language Bindings, Auth Patterns, and Streaming Resume
creator: Evelyn Park
description:
Summary: We need an operational rubric and a repeatable intake playbook for triaging SDK and client library requests coming from enterprise customers. Recent signals show rising demand for non-JS language bindings (Go, Rust, .NET), clearer enterprise auth patterns (SSO/SAML integration, token rotation, KMS-backed secrets), and robust streaming ergonomics (reconnect+resume, backpressure, chunk checkpoints). Goal: produce a single-page governance rubric for intake, a prioritization scoring matrix, and recommended engineering implementation patterns (with small-surface reference implementations) that satisfy enterprise security and observability requirements.

Background & customer signals:
- Enterprise pilots from three accounts (Acme Corp, NovaHealth, FinEdge Capital) requested first-class Go and Rust client libraries with streaming session resume and SSO support.
- Solutions engineering notes: several customers currently proxy through server-side adapters to handle token rotation; this increases latency and operational burden.
- Sales asks: provide an onramp checklist for customers that shows which SDKs are roadmap vs supported and clear trade-offs.

Scope:
- Evaluate and categorize language binding requests by strategic value, maintenance cost, and risk.
- Define auth patterns to standardize: bearer token refresh, SAML/SSO implicit flows, service account KMS-backed credentials, rotating short-lived tokens for streaming.
- Define streaming ergonomics baseline: reconnect strategy (exponential backoff + resume token), ACK/sequence checkpointing, client-side backpressure primitives, and clear server-stated guarantees (at-most-once vs at-least-once).
- Produce 2 reference implementations: Go SDK (streaming + resumable session) and lightweight server-side adapter pattern for on-prem/VPC customers.

Trade-offs considered:
- API simplicity vs security: a single ergonomic streaming API may hide token rotation complexity; prefer explicit session lifecycle primitives with helper utilities.
- Maintenance overhead: each additional language increases test surface; require a minimum engagement rubric (adoption, paid customer demand, cross-team ownership).
- Latency vs reliability: buffering to smooth throughput can increase perceived latency; recommend opt-in batching with default low-latency path.

Acceptance criteria (high-level):
- Governance rubric published in Confluence with scoring thresholds (accept/prioritize/defer) and examples.
- Prioritization matrix implemented as a canonical spreadsheet and linked in intake flow.
- Two reference artifacts merged: a Go SDK streaming PR and an adapter pattern doc.
- Security review checklist included and sign-off from Security and Compliance.
- A single-line internal route for requests: intake -> triage meeting -> prioritized backlog entry with owner.

Links & references:
- Intake form (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.example.com/display/SDK/SDK+Intake+Form
- Draft Go SDK PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-go/pull/312
- Streaming ergonomics design doc (drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1z-StreamDesign

notes: Proposal recommends a hard gating threshold: at least one paying customer + cross-functional owner or 3+ high intent signals before greenlighting a new language binding. Use scoring matrix: (customer_count * 3) + (strategic_fit * 2) + (maintenance_cost_inverse * 1) - (security_risk * 2).
